p: Before you even get inside, have a look at the great bronze knocker on the north door. The one there now is a replica, but it stands for something brilliant: in medieval times a fugitive who reached the cathedral could claim sanctuary, buying themselves time to sort out their fate. It's a cracking story to tell the kids as you push the door open.

Once you're in, don't leave without finding the Galilee Chapel at the western end, where Bede is buried, and the shrine of St Cuthbert behind the high altar. Then step out into the cloisters. If they look oddly familiar, that's because they turned up in the early Harry Potter films, and young wizards love walking the same stone corridors. The Open Treasure exhibition, in the old monastic buildings, takes you through spaces such as the monks' dormitory and the great kitchen, and shows off treasures linked to St Cuthbert. It's run separately from the free general visit, so decide if it's for you.

Allow at least an hour for the cathedral itself and longer if you add the exhibition or the tower. Comfy shoes are a must, because the peninsula is steep and cobbled. Afterwards, take the riverside path down towards Prebends Bridge for the classic view of the cathedral rising above the trees, then wander across Palace Green to admire Durham Castle, now part of the university. It's one of those cities where the walk between sights is half the joy.
